The other two samples yielded single domain results; one came from a dunite and the other from an antigorite-bearing rock and both carried an A component. These results therefore, reflect the abundant multidomain grain size of the magnetite seen in thin section. It has been suggested by Lienert & Wasilewski (1979) that Ni,Fe is a common carrier of remanence in this type of ultramafites and that this mineral has similar properties to magnetite but is distinguishable from magnetite on the grounds of its higher (590°C) Curie point. No Curie points above 580 "C were noted in this study suggesting that this phase is not present in significant amounts in these ultramafites. The net result of all these experiments was that no detectable difference in magnetic characteristics exists between different rock types carrying the same component direction or the same rock type carrying different magnetic components. All of these rocks have suffered late stage greenschist metamorphism which has produced chlorite as the dominant -Fe-bearing phase; this metamorphism may have been responsible for the alteration of any original magnetite present. In contrast, the serpentinised ultra- mafites tend to have large NRM intensities, often in excess of 1Am-1, and high bulk susceptibilities reflecting the relatively high modal content (1-5 per cent) of magnetite in these rocks. Magnetite is optically observed to occur in three common forms namely, (i) large skeletal grains, (ii) fine dusts and clusters of small grains in association with serpentine alteration products after olivine and pyroxene, and (iii) as irregular trains of crystals in serpentine veins which cross-cut each other and all earlier fabrics. pole and be either of middle to upper Devonian age or Siluro-Devonian in age. 6 CONCLUSIONS Three distinct magnetizations have been isolated from the ultramafite units of the Shetland ophiolite complex. All three have similar magnetic properties and showed no preferential stability with respect to each other. The broad range of temperature blocking spectra and low to medium median destruction fields would tend to suggest that all three magnetizations have similar origins. The most likely mechanism for producing these magnetizations in these rocks is thermo-chemical magnetization caused by serpen- tinisation, or alteration of the magnetite originally produced by serpentinisation. This would explain why only the serpentinised ultramafites in this complex carry a significant remanence. The dominant A component is most likely to be the oldest remanence and to have an Ordovician age because it does not correlate with the post-lower Silurian field in this region, but this cannot be confirmed as yet. The B component direction has been assigned a tentative Siluro-Devonian age and the C component a mid- Carboniferous age. Two of the four sites with stable remanence directions (sites 35 and 62) that were excluded from the overall mean directional analysis have directions cl

boniferous age. Two of the four sites with stable remanence directions (sites 35 and 62) that were excluded from the overall mean directional analysis have directions close to components attributed to a primary upper-middle ORS (upper Devonian-lower Carboniferous) origin by Robinson (1985). Clearly palaeomagnetism has detected a number of subtle events of differing age which appear to be of thermo-chemical origin as opposed to primary TRM. This suggests that the processes responsible for serpentinisation of the complex continued to occur long after tectonic emplacement, or that subtle low-temperature alteration events affected the magnetite grains initially formed by serpentinisation. Such alteration events are likely to have been due to either tectonic or climatic processes, for example Devonian strike-slip motions or permo- Carboniferous weathering regimes. If this is the case then it is most likely to be of Ordovician age as this is the least constrained time period. Inclusion of such a pole into the APW path demands a radical new path to that previously supposed, although this may yet prove to be tenable (Piper, pers. comm.). (2a) The complex as a whole and hence also the magnetization direction have been rotated about a non-vertical axis leading to the displacement of the palaeopole from the APW path. (2b) The complex is a far travelled displaced terrane, such that it has undergone translation subsequent to thrust stacking of the nappes and acquisition of the A component magnetization. All three have similar magnetic properties and showed no preferential stability with respect to each other. The broad range of temperature blocking spectra and low to medium median destruction fields would tend to suggest that all three magnetizations have similar origins. The most likely mechanism for producing these magnetizations in these rocks is thermo-chemical magnetization caused by serpen- tinisation, or alteration of the magnetite originally produced by serpentinisation. This would explain why only the serpentinised ultramafites in this complex carry a significant remanence. The dominant A component is most likely to be the oldest remanence and to have an Ordovician age because it does not correlate with the post-lower Silurian field in this region, but this cannot be confirmed as yet. The B component direction has been assigned a tentative Siluro-Devonian age and the C component a mid- Carboniferous age. Two of the four sites with stable remanence directions (sites 35 and 62) that were excluded from the overall mean directional analysis have directions cl

boniferous age. Two of the four sites with stable remanence directions (sites 35 and 62) that were excluded from the overall mean directional analysis have directions close to components attributed to a primary upper-middle ORS (upper Devonian-lower Carboniferous) origin by Robinson (1985). Clearly palaeomagnetism has detected a number of subtle events of differing age which appear to be of thermo-chemical origin as opposed to primary TRM. This suggests that the processes responsible for serpentinisation of the complex continued to occur long after tectonic emplacement, or that subtle low-temperature alteration events affected the magnetite grains initially formed by serpentinisation. Such alteration events are likely to have been due to either tectonic or climatic processes, for example Devonian strike-slip motions or permo- Carboniferous weathering regimes. Of these only 35 sites from the ultramafite facies of the complex yielded statistically significant results. These sites define three distinct populations of mag- netization directions which correspond to south palaeomagnetic poles at 47.2"s 244.2"E (A), 18.0"s 323.4"E (B), and 35.0"s 351.1"E (C). Of these only the C remanence can be assigned an unambiguous age of mid-Carboniferous; the ages of the other two poles remain ambiguous due to the uncertainty in the APW path and the complexity of the ophiolite history. The complex consists essentially of two ophiolitic thrust nappes separated from each other and the underlying basement rocks by melanges of both tectonic and sedimentary origin (Fig. 1). The basement to the area comprises heterogeneous schists and gneisses which have been equated with the Lower Dalradian Succession of Scotland (Flinn et al. 1972). This basement is overlain by thrust sheets composed of metasediments (the Saxa Vord block of Fig. 1) which have been interpreted (Flinn 1958) as being emplaced prior to the ophiolite complex thrust sheets. The lower ophiolitic thrust nappe contains a classic ophiolite sequence comprising mantle harzburgite overlain in turn by a transitional layered harzburgite-dunite unit, massive dunite, clinopyroxenite (often a wehrlite) and finally gabbro. The lower ophiolitic thrust nappe contains a classic ophiolite sequence comprising mantle harzburgite overlain in turn by a transitional layered harzburgite-dunite unit, massive dunite, clinopyroxenite (often a wehrlite) and finally gabbro. Many of these units are banded or layered both at the main lithological boundaries and internally. In addition dolerite dykes, plagigranites and metavolcanics have all been recorded from the lower thrust nappe to provide a complete representation of all the members of a normal ophiolite sequence. All three have similar magnetic properties and showed no preferential stability with respect to each other. The broad range of temperature blocking spectra and low to medium median destruction fields would tend to suggest that all three magnetizations have similar origins. The most likely mechanism for producing these magnetizations in these rocks is thermo-chemical magnetization caused by serpen- tinisation, or alteration of the magnetite originally produced by serpentinisation. This would explain why only the serpentinised ultramafites in this complex carry a significant remanence. The dominant A component is most likely to be the oldest remanence and to have an Ordovician age because it does not correlate with the post-lower Silurian field in this region, but this cannot be confirmed as yet. The B component direction has been assigned a tentative Siluro-Devonian age and the C component a mid- Carboniferous age. Two of the four sites with stable remanence directions (sites 35 and 62) that were excluded from the overall mean directional analysis have directions cl

boniferous age. Two of the four sites with stable remanence directions (sites 35 and 62) that were excluded from the overall mean directional analysis have directions close to components attributed to a primary upper-middle ORS (upper Devonian-lower Carboniferous) origin by Robinson (1985). Clearly palaeomagnetism has detected a number of subtle events of differing age which appear to be of thermo-chemical origin as opposed to primary TRM. This suggests that the processes responsible for serpentinisation of the complex continued to occur long after tectonic emplacement, or that subtle low-temperature alteration events affected the magnetite grains initially formed by serpentinisation. Such alteration events are likely to have been due to either tectonic or climatic processes, for example Devonian strike-slip motions or permo- Carboniferous weathering regimes. Of these only 35 sites from the ultramafite facies of the complex yielded statistically significant results. These sites define three distinct populations of mag- netization directions which correspond to south palaeomagnetic poles at 47.2"s 244.2"E (A), 18.0"s 323.4"E (B), and 35.0"s 351.1"E (C). Of these only the C remanence can be assigned an unambiguous age of mid-Carboniferous; the ages of the other two poles remain ambiguous due to the uncertainty in the APW path and the complexity of the ophiolite history. The lower ophiolitic thrust nappe contains a classic ophiolite sequence comprising mantle harzburgite overlain in turn by a transitional layered harzburgite-dunite unit, massive dunite, clinopyroxenite (often a wehrlite) and finally gabbro. Many of these units are banded or layered both at the main lithological boundaries and internally. In addition dolerite dykes, plagigranites and metavolcanics have all been recorded from the lower thrust nappe to provide a complete representation of all the members of a normal ophiolite sequence. The upper ophiolitic thrust nappe consists predominantly of harzburgite, with occasional lenses of dunite, which is commonly found to be banded or layered. After magnetic cleaning, a weak but stable primary NRM with high coercivities and high unblocking temperatures was isolated, with D = 157", I = +52" (k = 118, mg5 = 3", N = 20). The corresponding virtual geomagnetic pole (VGP) is 4"S, 93"W (dp = 3", dm = 4"), which falls on the North American apparent polar wander path around 1850 Ma. The basement of this part of Alberta is probably an extension of the Churchill Structural Province of the Laurentian Shield. Other possible large-scale tectonic deformations in the Andes have been highlighted by palaeomagnetic studies in the northernmost (MacDonald & Opdyke 1972; Roperch et af. 1987) and southernmost parts (Bums et af. 1980; Dalziel et af. 1973). rmation (Table 1). 6 FOLD TESTS IN THE SALROCK REGION The sampled section in the Salrock Formation includes two internally uniform structural units: the strata in both units dip moderately steeply towards the north, with cu. 12" difference in average orientation. The stratigraphically lower unit occupies the ground between sites S1 and S14, and the upper unit between sites S34 and S16 (Fig. 2, Table 1). The strike and dip of bedding measured at each site are given in Table 1; and the 'folded' and 'unfolded' site mean component H and I directions are shown in Fig. 6(a, b). Component H directions from site S15 are excluded from the fold test analysis due to their apparent reorientation associated with local thrusting and cleavage development in addition to folding. It records a cycle of marine transgression and regression within a marginal marine and fluviatile sedimentary environment. The petrography of the clastics indicates a northerly sediment source which can no longer be identified to the north of Clare Island (Phillips 1974). Similarly, volcanic rocks on Clare Island provide evidence of northerly provenance but no source area survives. This can most readily be explained by strike-slip displacement on the Clew Bay fault zone and/or the Leck fault (Figs 1 and 3). Max & Riddihough (1975) and Max, Ryan & Indamdar (1983) suggest that the faults cutting across Ireland to emerge at Clew Bay are a continuation of the Highland Boundary Fault of Scotland. Ireland at latitude 1.6"S, longitude 287.7"E (dp = 2S0, dm = 4.6", N = 27 sites). A further 12 sampling sites were located in Silurian redbeds on Clare Island, S. Mayo where a palaeomagnetic remanence of Silurian age was also identified. Both remanences pre-date local late-Caledonian folding. Morris (1973) carried out some alternating field (AF) cleaning of samples from two sections through the Salrock Formation, a sequence consisting predominantly of red siltstones. Although there is reason to believe that his study failed to resolve the multicomponent NRM satisfactorily, it nevertheless revealed the potential of these rocks as ancient remanence carriers. Therefore the Salrock Formation has been resampled, and a further suite of samples taken from structurally more complicated strata of similar age on Clare Island. Complete progressive demagnetisation has been applied to isolate components of NRM effectively. The Clare Island and Salrock regions lie 25 km apart, to the south and north respectively, of the Ordovician S Mayo Trough, an E-W trending tract of the non-metamorphic Caledonides. Palaeomagnetism of Silurian sediments in W Ireland: evidence for block rotation in the Caledonides M. A. Smethurst" and J. C. Brident Department of Earth Sciences, University of Leeds, Lee& LS2 9JT, UK Accepted 1988 May 20. Received 1988 May 9; in original form 1987 November 25 SUMMARY A palaeomagnetic study of mid-Silurian (Wenlock) sediments of the Salrock Formation in NW Galway yields a reliable Silurian palaeomagnetic pole position for W. Ireland at latitude 1.6"S, longitude 287.7"E (dp = 2S0, dm = 4.6", N = 27 sites). A further 12 sampling sites were located in Silurian redbeds on Clare Island, S. Mayo where a palaeomagnetic remanence of Silurian age was also identified. Both remanences pre-date local late-Caledonian folding. However the Clare Island result has an anomalous azimuth when compared with the Salrock result and with published Silurian results for Britain. The two Irish results can be reconciled by anticlockwise block rotation of the Clare Island region through 40"-SO". The rotation brings both palaeomagnetic and structural trends within the two sampling regions into alignment. Strike-slip displacement across the Clew Bay fault zone, producing a sinistral shear couple, might have enabled such a rotation. The timing and geographic extent of the proposed b

nd provide an opportunity to add to the currently limited number of reliable Siluro-Devonian pole positions for this part of the British Isles. For a recent summary of the most reliable Siluro-Devonian pole positions currently available for Britain see Livermore, Smith & Briden (1985). Morris (1973) carried out some alternating field (AF) cleaning of samples from two sections through the Salrock Formation, a sequence consisting predominantly of red siltstones. Although there is reason to believe that his study failed to resolve the multicomponent NRM satisfactorily, it nevertheless revealed the potential of these rocks as ancient remanence carriers. Therefore the Salrock Formation has been resampled, and a further suite of samples taken from structurally more complicated strata of similar age on Clare Island. Complete progressive demagnetisation has been applied to isolate components of NRM effectively. The Clare Island and Salrock regions lie 25 km apart, to the south and north respectively, of the Ordovician S Mayo Trough, an E-W trending tract of the non-metamorphic Caledonides. The trough is approximately 25 km wide (the distance between Salrock and Clare Island). It is bounded both to the north and (uniquely in the British Caledonides) to the south in Connemara

B4, PAGES 2953-2970, APRIL 10, 1981 Tillamook Volcanic Series' Further Evidence for Tectonic Rotation of the Oregon Coast Range JAMES MAGILL AND ALLAN Cox Department of Geophysics, Stanford University, Stanford, California 94305 ROBERT DUNCAN School of Oceanography, Oregon State University, Corvallis, Oregon 97331 Paleomagnetic directions from the Eocene Tillamook Volcanic Series of the Oregon Coast Range point 46 ø clockwise from the expected Eocene field direction. Potassium argon dating of six dikes and flows from this formation yields a mean age of 44.3 + 0.6 m.y. These results establish that the Oregon coastal block of Simpson and Cox (1977) extends north to the Oregon-Washington border and that this block has rotated clockwise 46 ø + 13 ø during the past 44 m.y. The block has undergone no detectable north-south translation. A two phase model is developed to explain the tectonic history and anomalous magnetic field directions of the Pacific northwest region. Phase I of the rotation, active between 50 and 42 m.y.B.P., results from fragmentation of the Farallon plate with rotation of a fragment during its accre- tion to North Am

Phase II of the rotation, active between 20 m.y.b.p. and the present, occurs in association with extension in the Basin and Range province. INTRODUCTION Anomalous directions of magnetization in early Tertiary rocks of the Coast Range of Oregon (Figure 1), first reported by Cox [1957] and confirmed by recent paleomagnetic studies [Simpson and Cox, 1977], have established that lower, middle, and upper Eocene sedimentary and volcanic rocks have un- dergone dockwise rotations about vertical axes of from 50 ø to 75 ø (Figure 2). The area sampled in these studies is a block extending northward 225 km from the Klamath Mountains. The fact that similar dockwise rotations are recorded in rocks of varying Eocene age and as petrologically dissimilar as ba- salts and turbidites leaves little doubt that the anomalous paleomagnetic directions have recorded a true tectonic rota- tion. Having established this, however, a number of questions remain concerning the regional extent and timing of the rota- tions and the mechanisms responsible for them. The analysis of the results obtained by structural and paleomagnetic studies on 14 sites leads to the following observations: in most sites, the mean direction of the strain shortening axis is close to the expected Permian paleomagnetic direction. ands [51 Tertiary geodynamical evolution of northwestern Greece: paleomagnetic results Catherine Kissel 1 Carlo Laj 1 and Carla Mialler 2 1Centre des Faibles Radioactivitks, Domaine du CNRS, 91190 Gif -sur-Yvette (France) el Rue Martignon, 92500 Rueil- Malmaison (France) Received July 1, 1984 Revised version accepted November 19, 1984 Paleomagnetic results have been obtained from 29 sites sampled in Lower to Upper Oligocene flysch sections of the Ionian Zone in northwestern Greece. They indicate a clockwise rotation of about 450 of the entire region. A comparison with previously published results relative to both younger and older formations shows that this rotation has occurred in two phases of comparable amplitude, one during Middle Miocene and the other during Pliocene and Quaternary, separated by a period of at least 7 Ma during which no significant rotation has occurred. No major rotation has occurred during the entire Paleocene and Eocene stages. This large measured rotation implies a horizontal displacement of at least 100 km in Epirus. Possible mechanisms involving a rotation of the nappe sheets, rotation of the basement or a combination of the two are discussed. f paleomagnetic rotation can be correlated with the Tertiary and Quaternary calc-alkaline volcanic activity in the Aegean Sea. A palinspastic reconstruction shows that the orientation of the major structures, now striking N155 °, was almost east-west in the Middle Miocene at the epoch of their formation. 1. Introduction During the last three decades many important geological studies have documented the Tertiary evolution of the Hellenides and the collision of the Adriatic plate with the Rhodope massif. Although, the exact timing and the detailed mechanisms of the collision and of the post-collision evolution are still a subject of discussion, there is a general agreement that a large scale, westward directed thrusting occurred on Triassic evaporitic horizons, which resulted in the emplacement of nappe sheets over the Apulian platform. The last major phase of the "Alpine" activity in northwestern Greece oc- curred during Mid-Miocene [1]. Moreover, in the last 10 or 15 years, neotectonic and geophysical studies have provided new data and ideas about the most recent geodynamical evolution of the Aegean Area. Seismic studies, for 0012-821X/85/$03.30 © 1985 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. instance, leave little doubt about the existence, in the southern part of the Aege

o significant rotation of the south- eastern part of the arc has occurred since the Late Tortonian. On the other hand, results from the Ionian Islands [5,10] yield evidence of 25 ° clock- wise rotation with respect to the present geo- graphic pole since the Mio-Pliocene boundary. While no significant rotation of this region was detected between the Serravallian-Tortonian and the Mio-Pliocene boundaries, preliminary results from 16 Oligocene flysch sections in the Ionian Zone [11] indicate an earlier phase of some 25-30 ° additional clockwise rotation. Also, Horner and Freeman [12] obtained precise paleomagnetic re- suits from 51 sites sampled in the Paleocene and Eocene "microbreccious limestones" of the Ionian Zone which indicate a 38 ° clockwise rotation of this region since Upper Eocene. In this paper, we report additional paleomag- netic results obtained from lower to Upper Oligo- cene flysch sections in the Ionian Zone, both in Epirus and Akarnania. A comparison of these results with the above-mentioned paleomagnetic results within the framework of known geological data then allows a fairly complete description of the geodynamical evolution of northwestern Greece for the entire Tertiary and Quaternary periods. 2. Also shown are the locations of nearby monoclines on the Colorado Plateau [8]. The Rock Canyon monocline is an east-facing fold which can be traced some 7 km and is the only monocline in the Salt River Canyon for which both hinge zones are exposed [4]. The monocline displays a minimum of 90 m of structural relief, trends about N22°W, and locally plunges about 10 ° towards S20°E [3,4]. Upper Proterozoic Apache Group sedimentary rocks, including the Mescal Limestone and the Dripping Spring Quartzite, are deformed by the Rock Creek mono- cline. The diabase sill exposed in the monocline intrudes the Dripping Spring Quartzite and is just one element of an extensive complex of sills that have intruded Apache Group sedimentary rocks in the Salt River Canyon area. Thickness of the di- abase sill in the Rock Canyon monocline is about 100 m. Five sites of conglomerate, sandstone and limestone reveal a stable component of magnetization (D = 43 °, /= 43°; a95 = 7.5°). We argue that this component is of primary origin on the basis of a positive fold test, observation of both normal and reversed directions and a reported magnetostratigraphy from Middle Triassic to Cretaceous. This unit is found to have remained at tropical northern latitudes since the Upper Triassic. Comparison with Eurasian poles reveals 1650 ± 850 km of SW-NE convergence and 15 ° + 10 ° of counterclockwise rotation between 205 and 160 Ma. Two mechanisms are discussed to account for this motion. Introduction With the emergence of a significant amount of palaeomagnetic data derived from stepwise de- magnetization, it is now feasible to investigate the palaeomagnetic record of metamorphic terrains to obtain information on the thermal and structural history. Palaeomagnetic data are available from Precambrian metamorphic terrains but these stud- ies generally emphasize the construction of por- tions of polar wander paths. In this paper I pre- sent palaeomagnetic results from haematite schists in the staurolite and kyanite zones of Glen Esk and Glen Lethnot, Angus, Scotland, within the area where Barrow [1,2] demonstrated the ex- istence of zones of progressive regional metamor- phism. Improvement of paleomagnetic data sug- gests that the rotation of Southwest Japan relative to the Eurasia started later than 21 Ma. This result gives rise to the hypothesis on the Miocene origin 266 of rifting of the Japan arc. The present investigation is focused on the Northeast Japan arc: The study was undertaken to discover the paleomagnetic evidence for the Miocene counter-clockwise rotation of the North- east Japan arc in an attempt to determine the timing of rifting of the Japan arc. 2. Geology and sampling Four different stages can be distinguished for igneous activity in Northeast Japan since the Cretaceous [19,20]. Granites and granodiorites of Cretaceous to early Paleogene age, felsic igneous rocks of Paleogene age, the "Green Tuff" of late Tertiary age, and andesitic materials of late Miocene to the Present resulted from four respec- tive stages of activity (see Fig. 1). Intrusion of plutons commenced in the late stage of Early Cretaceous throughout the entire region of North- east Japan, e.g., Kitakami, Abukuma, Ashio and Iide-Asahi. The plutonic activity took place at first in the Pacific coast side at 110-120 Ma and the active area subsequently shifted toward the Japan Sea side. In the early Paleogene period (50-65 Ma), the plutonic rocks acc

arly Paleogene period (50-65 Ma), the plutonic rocks accompanied with the felsic volcanic rocks occurred in the Uetsu area which extends from Tsukuba, northward through Asahi to Oga Peninsula. Intensive volcanism was reactivated in the western side of Northeast Japan since late Oligocene. Their volcanic products called "Green Tuff" are dominated by a series of pyro- clastic rocks, in which some constituents are al- tered to chlorite, epidote, sericite and zeolite. The green tuff volcanism was initiated by voluminous intermediate and acidic volcanic rocks in the sub- aerial environment, and followed by lesser amounts of submarine basalts and andesites. The andesitic magma erupted over the Ou Mountain Range in the central part of Northeast Japan during late Miocene to the Present. Our paleomagnetic approach is to analyze the welded tufts of Paleogene to Miocene age, because a reliable remanent magnetization could be ex- pected to be obtained [16,21,22] and tilting of the welded tuff could be corrected on the basis of the eutaxitic structure (lineation of stretched pumice and aligned phenocrysts) [23]. . The previous models [12,14] based on the paleomagnetic data obtained before 1980 suggested that the Japan arc had been straight in figure before both arcs under- went the differential rotation. Since our study and the recent paleomagnetic works, in which the data are obtained after the treatments of thermal de- magnetization and tilt correction, have produced accurate estimate of the amount of rotation for both Northeast and Southwest Japan arcs, a <- shape is a more realistic estimate for the paleoshape of the Japan arc than the straight figure. This inference is supported by geometrical fitting: the < -shape of Japan arc is fairly similar to the shape of the coast line from Sikhote Alin to the Korean Peninsula. We delineate the process for rotation of both parts of Japanese islands as follows: The eastern margin of the Asian continent was subjected to a force (indicated by a large arrow in Fig. 7) exerted either from the eastward flow of the asthenosphere with respect to the continental lithosphere [47,48] or the tectonic flow induced by downgoing slab [49] at the Miocene period. Since both Northeast Japan and Southwest Japan at the continental margin had thinner lithosphere than the Korean Peninsula and China [50-52], the lithosphere be- low both part

orean Peninsula and China [50-52], the lithosphere be- low both parts of Japan was not strong enough to resist the active extension. Both parts, therefore, rifted from the continent. Southwest Japan rotated clockwise and Northeast Japan counter-clockwise at about 15 Ma. The diamond shaped back arc basin, the Japan Sea, was created by the differen- tial rotation of the two parts of Japan [53]. The Japan arc consists of several geologic ter- ranes, which are zonally arranged sub-parallel to the Japan trench or parallel to the Nankai Trough [54]. When the primary block of the Japan arc at the continental margin was subjected to the force which rifted the block from the continental margin, these terranes prior to rifting probably behaved as a pile of elastic planks (see Fig. 7). Sliding at the boundaries of the terranes will take place. The remanent magnetizations of welded tufts with age between 32 Ma and 21 Ma old from 17 widely distributed sampling sites in Northeast Japan are fairly well grouped with a mean of D = -41.2 °, I = 56.5 °, ot95 = 7.2 °. The remanent magnetization of welded tufts of 14 Ma and 11 Ma from 4 sites shows a northerly direction (D = -11.7 °, 1 = 60.5 °, a95 = 15.3°). These data imply that Northeast Japan was apparently subjected to a counter-clockwise rotation through 47_+ 14 ° about a vertical axis on the representative

Improvement of paleomagnetic data sug- gests that the rotation of Southwest Japan relative to the Eurasia started later than 21 Ma. This result gives rise to the hypothesis on the Miocene origin 266 of rifting of the Japan arc. The present investigation is focused on the Northeast Japan arc: The study was undertaken to discover the paleomagnetic evidence for the Miocene counter-clockwise rotation of the North- east Japan arc in an attempt to determine the timing of rifting of the Japan arc. 2. Geology and sampling Four different stages can be distinguished for igneous activity in Northeast Japan since the Cretaceous [19,20]. Granites and granodiorites of Cretaceous to early Paleogene age, felsic igneous rocks of Paleogene age, the "Green Tuff" of late Tertiary age, and andesitic materials of late Miocene to the Present resulted from four respec- tive stages of activity (see Fig. 1). Intrusion of plutons commenced in the late stage of Early Cretaceous throughout the entire region of North- east Japan, e.g., Kitakami, Abukuma, Ashio and Iide-Asahi. The plutonic activity took place at first in the Pacific coast side at 110-120 Ma and the active area subsequently shifted toward the Japan Sea side. In the early Paleogene period (50-65 Ma), the plutonic rocks acc

arly Paleogene period (50-65 Ma), the plutonic rocks accompanied with the felsic volcanic rocks occurred in the Uetsu area which extends from Tsukuba, northward through Asahi to Oga Peninsula. Intensive volcanism was reactivated in the western side of Northeast Japan since late Oligocene. Their volcanic products called "Green Tuff" are dominated by a series of pyro- clastic rocks, in which some constituents are al- tered to chlorite, epidote, sericite and zeolite. The green tuff volcanism was initiated by voluminous intermediate and acidic volcanic rocks in the sub- aerial environment, and followed by lesser amounts of submarine basalts and andesites. The andesitic magma erupted over the Ou Mountain Range in the central part of Northeast Japan during late Miocene to the Present. Our paleomagnetic approach is to analyze the welded tufts of Paleogene to Miocene age, because a reliable remanent magnetization could be ex- pected to be obtained [16,21,22] and tilting of the welded tuff could be corrected on the basis of the eutaxitic structure (lineation of stretched pumice and aligned phenocrysts) [23]. section_candidates.excerpt: Improvement of paleomagnetic data sug- gests that the rotation of Southwest Japan relative to the Eurasia started later than 21 Ma. This result gives rise to the hypothesis on the Miocene origin 266 of rifting of the Japan arc. The present investigation is focused on the Northeast Japan arc: The study was undertaken to discover the paleomagnetic evidence for the Miocene counter-clockwise rotation of the North- east Japan arc in an attempt to determine the timing of rifting of the Japan arc. 2. Geology and sampling Four different stages can be distinguished for igneous activity in Northeast Japan since the Cretaceous [19,20]. Granites and granodiorites of Cretaceous to early Paleogene age, felsic igneous rocks of Paleogene age, the "Green Tuff" of late Tertiary age, and andesitic materials of late Miocene to the Present resulted from four respec- tive stages of activity (see Fig. 1). Intrusion of plutons commenced in the late stage of Early Cretaceous throughout the entire region of North- east Japan, e.g., Kitakami, Abukuma, Ashio and Iide-Asahi. The plutonic activity took place at first in the Pacific coast side at 110-120 Ma and the active area subsequently shifted toward the Japan Sea side. Aside from alteration geometries and fluid origins, stable isotope ratios of rocks and minerals can also indi- cate water/rock ratios [15,17] and time-integrated temperature histories of fluid-rock interactions [18-20]. Because many subsolidus chemical changes of rocks occur in the presence of an aqueous fluid, stable isotope studies in conjunc- tion with paleomagnetic and rock magnetic ex- periments may provide insights into the impor- tance of CRM in igneous rocks. This study combines paleomagnetic and rock magnetic data with stable isotope data from mag- netic and silicate minerals and whole rocks in an effort to delineate the processes of magnetization during the crystallization and cooling of granitic rocks. Rb-Sr mineral isochron ages of 26 m.y. de- termined on rocks from Hondo Canyon and the Columbine Creek drainage, support this interpre- tation (C. Johnson, unpublished data, 1984). Younger plutons emplaced to the north of the Rio Hondo pluton include the Sulfur Gulch and the Bear Canyon plutons (Fig. 1). These plutons intrude the Tertiary intracaldera volcanic rocks and Precambrian wall rocks along the southern margin of the Questa caldera. The Sulfur Gulch and Bear Canyon plutons consist of high-silica porphyritic to medium-grained granite and aplite, with sparse biotite. Both plutons have been hydro- thermally altered and contain local pyrite, fluorite and molybdenite mineralization which reaches economic levels in the Sulfur Gulch pluton [25]. Recalculated K-Ar biotite ages on both plutons and the mineralization cluster around 23 m.y. [26,27]. Exposed to the south of the Rio Hondo pluton is the medium-grained equigranular granite of Lucero Peak. Introduction It has been proposed that many tectonic fea- tures observed in central and southeastern Asia can be understood as direct consequences of the collision of the rigid Indian continent with the southern margin of the Asia continent commenc- ing in the early Tertiary [1,2]. The possibility that continental blocks of eastern Asia have undergone rotation and translation during the Cenozoic can be tested by paleomagnetic studies. Paleomagnetic constraints on Late Cretaceous and Cenozoic tectonics of southeastern Asia have been recently reviewed by Achache et al. [3]. There is only a single paleomagnetic result for the Creta- ceous of South China and it is based on samples not subjected to magnetic cleaning [4]. Introduction It has been proposed that many tectonic fea- tures observed in central and southeastern Asia can be understood as direct consequences of the collision of the rigid Indian continent with the southern margin of the Asia continent commenc- ing in the early Tertiary [1,2]. The possibility that continental blocks of eastern Asia have undergone rotation and translation during the Cenozoic can be tested by paleomagnetic studies. Paleomagnetic constraints on Late Cretaceous and Cenozoic tectonics of southeastern Asia have been recently reviewed by Achache et al. [3]. There is only a single paleomagnetic result for the Creta- ceous of South China and it is based on samples not subjected to magnetic cleaning [4]. Conclusions (1) The mean pole positions for Pliocene and Upper Miocene volcanic rocks from Fernando de Noronha (Quixaba Formation, Rem6dios and Sao Jos~ Formations, respectively) are different from each other. This was not recognized in previous studies. (2) The ferrimagnetic minerals are titanomag- netites, many of which have undergone high-tem- perature oxidation. This implies subaerial erup- tion. Most samples have also undergone low-tem- perature oxidation of various degree. (3) The initial titanomagnetites (before high- temperature oxidation) have in most cases a com- position with x = 0.6, for the Rem6dios Forma- tion in some cases with x = 0.2. (4) The hysteresis parameters measured can be interpreted in terms of PSD structure for the Quixaba and S~o Jos6 Formation and PSD and MD structure for the Rem6dios Formation. The stability of remanence is moderate and somewhat weaker for the Rem6dios

section_candidates.excerpt: accepted April 16, 1986 Seven sites from basaltic rocks of the Quixaba Formation (K/Ar age 3.4 ± 1.7 m.y.) on Fernando de Noronha (3.85°S, 32.4°W) yield a pole at 80.3°N, 234oE with Ags - 2.9 ° and K = 446 after AF cleaning, and seven sites from the Remfidios Formation (9.5 ± 1.1 m.y.) yield a pole at 84.5°N, 136°E with A~5 - 7,5 ° and K= 65. Combination of all published reliable data results in poles at 80.6ON, 216°E (N=21, Ags=3.2 ° , K=I00) and 86.0ON, 81°E (N = 17, Ags = 4.9 °, K = 53) for the Quixaba and Rem6dios Formation, respectively (both with mixed polarity). The two pole positions differ significantly from each other. Seven sites from volcanics (K/Ar age 28.7 + 2.5 m.y.) in the province of Fortaleza (3.8°S, 38.7°W) yield a pole at 66°N, 54OE with /195 ~ 19.1 ° and K= 10.9. Rock magnetic investigations and chemical analyses on samples from Fernando de Noronha reveal as primary phase titanomagnetites with about 60% ulv/Sspinel in most cases. The titanomagnetites have undergone high-temperature oxidation and low-temperature oxidation of various degrees. The ferrimagnetic phases in the samples from the province of Fortaleza are magnetites with low-temperature alterations showing relative weak stability of remanence. 1. Introduction The Atlantic island Fernando de Noronha (Fig. 1) is about 365 km northeast of Natal, Rio Grande do Norte, Brazil. The island constitutes the east- ern end of a chain of volcanic seamounts. At the western end on the continent near Fortaleza (Cearfi) volcanism is also found. There are similar- ities in the volcanic activities in both areas [1]. In this paper data on palaeomagnetism and rock magnetism of Tertiary volcanic rocks near For- taleza and from Fernando de Noronha are pre- sented. Rock magnetic studies In order to identify the magnetic minerals several investigations were carried out including the determination of thermomagnetic curves and hysteresis parameters, X-ray studies, ore mi- croscopy, and chemical analysis. The thermomag- netic curves Is(T ) were measured in air on whole rock samples (moderately crushed) in a field of about 1800 Oe by means of a magnetic balance. The lattice constants were determined in a Debye-Scherrer camera with Co radiation on mag- netically separated ore. The chemical analyses were carried out with a transmission electron micro- scope (TEM) with energy-dispersive equipment. Yet, despite decades of extensive geological work, still relatively little is known about the internal struc- ture, age, total duration and ultimately origin of the Deccan volcanism As far as Internal structure is concerned, the lava pile consists of rather thick (10-160 m) flat lying flows, with dips seldom exceeding 1 °, except near Bombay where dips of 5 o towards the sea are observed Therefore, altitude has often been used as a simple first-order stratlgraphic indication This ignores the possibility of faults, which are not easy to identify because of the nature of basalts and the conditions of outcrops Also, one must be aware that non-measurable dips not exceeding 1 ° may lead to altitude differences of many hundreds of meters over the distances of several hundred kilometers which are typically encountered in the Deccan. Geological setting Structural trends in the Western Himalayan Syntaxis change from NNW-SSE and NW-SE in the eastern limb of the syntaxls, to N-S and NE- SW in the western limb of the syntaxls (Fig. 1 [31,32]) In the outermost thrust zones this bend becomes acute and the structural trend turns nearly upon itself from NNW-SSE to NNE-SSW to con- tinue into a WSW trend in the Eastern Salt Range. This acute reentrant is of superficial nature only Its development is facilitated by detachment in the Potwar Plateau-Salt Range region of the suprastructure along Eocambnan evaporltes of the Salt Range Formation (or Saline Series, [33]). The MBT and the MCT which approach each other in outcrop in the eastern limb of the syntaxts, known there as Murree Thrust and Panjal Thrust respec- tively, continue with a northwestern strike in the basement northwest of the syntaxas as the Indus Kohistan Seisnuc Zone (IKSZ [34]) The Kahsrmr Basin has been thrusted south- westwards as part of the Panjal Nappe over the Panjal Thrust which surfaces at the foot of the Pit Panjal Range in the Jammu-Kashrmr region A palaeomagnet~c reconnaissance study of the Kashnur Basin [35] has shown that this over- thrusting was characterized by a Late Tertiary clockwi

shield The thrust-slice between the Panjal Thrust and the directly southwards adjacent Mur- ree Thrust is made up of a sequence of Late Palaeozoic Panjal Traps overlain by carbonate of the Subathu Group [36,37] Further south within the Jammu foothills, the Raasi Thrust (Fig 1) forms a major dislocation zone, along which the Murree Group and locally basement and overlying Subathu Group sediments have been overthrust to the south onto Slwallk Group sediments. Geological setting Structural trends in the Western Himalayan Syntaxis change from NNW-SSE and NW-SE in the eastern limb of the syntaxls, to N-S and NE- SW in the western limb of the syntaxls (Fig. 1 [31,32]) In the outermost thrust zones this bend becomes acute and the structural trend turns nearly upon itself from NNW-SSE to NNE-SSW to con- tinue into a WSW trend in the Eastern Salt Range. This acute reentrant is of superficial nature only Its development is facilitated by detachment in the Potwar Plateau-Salt Range region of the suprastructure along Eocambnan evaporltes of the Salt Range Formation (or Saline Series, [33]). The MBT and the MCT which approach each other in outcrop in the eastern limb of the syntaxts, known there as Murree Thrust and Panjal Thrust respec- tively, continue with a northwestern strike in the basement northwest of the syntaxas as the Indus Kohistan Seisnuc Zone (IKSZ [34]) The Kahsrmr Basin has been thrusted south- westwards as part of the Panjal Nappe over the Panjal Thrust which surfaces at the foot of the Pit Panjal Range in the Jammu-Kashrmr region A palaeomagnet~c reconnaissance study of the Kashnur Basin [35] has shown that this over- thrusting was characterized by a Late Tertiary clockwi

Geological setting Structural trends in the Western Himalayan Syntaxis change from NNW-SSE and NW-SE in the eastern limb of the syntaxls, to N-S and NE- SW in the western limb of the syntaxls (Fig. 1 [31,32]) In the outermost thrust zones this bend becomes acute and the structural trend turns nearly upon itself from NNW-SSE to NNE-SSW to con- tinue into a WSW trend in the Eastern Salt Range. This acute reentrant is of superficial nature only Its development is facilitated by detachment in the Potwar Plateau-Salt Range region of the suprastructure along Eocambnan evaporltes of the Salt Range Formation (or Saline Series, [33]). The MBT and the MCT which approach each other in outcrop in the eastern limb of the syntaxts, known there as Murree Thrust and Panjal Thrust respec- tively, continue with a northwestern strike in the basement northwest of the syntaxas as the Indus Kohistan Seisnuc Zone (IKSZ [34]) The Kahsrmr Basin has been thrusted south- westwards as part of the Panjal Nappe over the Panjal Thrust which surfaces at the foot of the Pit Panjal Range in the Jammu-Kashrmr region A palaeomagnet~c reconnaissance study of the Kashnur Basin [35] has shown that this over- thrusting was characterized by a Late Tertiary clockwi

shield The thrust-slice between the Panjal Thrust and the directly southwards adjacent Mur- ree Thrust is made up of a sequence of Late Palaeozoic Panjal Traps overlain by carbonate of the Subathu Group [36,37] Further south within the Jammu foothills, the Raasi Thrust (Fig 1) forms a major dislocation zone, along which the Murree Group and locally basement and overlying Subathu Group sediments have been overthrust to the south onto Slwallk Group sediments. Geological setting Structural trends in the Western Himalayan Syntaxis change from NNW-SSE and NW-SE in the eastern limb of the syntaxls, to N-S and NE- SW in the western limb of the syntaxls (Fig. 1 [31,32]) In the outermost thrust zones this bend becomes acute and the structural trend turns nearly upon itself from NNW-SSE to NNE-SSW to con- tinue into a WSW trend in the Eastern Salt Range. This acute reentrant is of superficial nature only Its development is facilitated by detachment in the Potwar Plateau-Salt Range region of the suprastructure along Eocambnan evaporltes of the Salt Range Formation (or Saline Series, [33]). The MBT and the MCT which approach each other in outcrop in the eastern limb of the syntaxts, known there as Murree Thrust and Panjal Thrust respec- tively, continue with a northwestern strike in the basement northwest of the syntaxas as the Indus Kohistan Seisnuc Zone (IKSZ [34]) The Kahsrmr Basin has been thrusted south- westwards as part of the Panjal Nappe over the Panjal Thrust which surfaces at the foot of the Pit Panjal Range in the Jammu-Kashrmr region A palaeomagnet~c reconnaissance study of the Kashnur Basin [35] has shown that this over- thrusting was characterized by a Late Tertiary clockwi

shield The thrust-slice between the Panjal Thrust and the directly southwards adjacent Mur- ree Thrust is made up of a sequence of Late Palaeozoic Panjal Traps overlain by carbonate of the Subathu Group [36,37] Further south within the Jammu foothills, the Raasi Thrust (Fig 1) forms a major dislocation zone, along which the Murree Group and locally basement and overlying Subathu Group sediments have been overthrust to the south onto Slwallk Group sediments. Geological setting Structural trends in the Western Himalayan Syntaxis change from NNW-SSE and NW-SE in the eastern limb of the syntaxls, to N-S and NE- SW in the western limb of the syntaxls (Fig. 1 [31,32]) In the outermost thrust zones this bend becomes acute and the structural trend turns nearly upon itself from NNW-SSE to NNE-SSW to con- tinue into a WSW trend in the Eastern Salt Range. This acute reentrant is of superficial nature only Its development is facilitated by detachment in the Potwar Plateau-Salt Range region of the suprastructure along Eocambnan evaporltes of the Salt Range Formation (or Saline Series, [33]). The MBT and the MCT which approach each other in outcrop in the eastern limb of the syntaxts, known there as Murree Thrust and Panjal Thrust respec- tively, continue with a northwestern strike in the basement northwest of the syntaxas as the Indus Kohistan Seisnuc Zone (IKSZ [34]) The Kahsrmr Basin has been thrusted south- westwards as part of the Panjal Nappe over the Panjal Thrust which surfaces at the foot of the Pit Panjal Range in the Jammu-Kashrmr region A palaeomagnet~c reconnaissance study of the Kashnur Basin [35] has shown that this over- thrusting was characterized by a Late Tertiary clockwi

A large amount of pyrite was found, revealed in polished sections when examined under a micro- scope in reflected light. The presence of magnetite, probably the main carrier of NRM, was observed during the heating of saturation IRM in a field-free space (Fig. 2b, c) and during thermal demagneti- zation of NRM (Fig. 3b, c). The saturation IRM of unheated samples (first curves) was so weak that it was difficult to exactly determine the value of the Curie temperature and to distinguish be- tween magnetite and maghemite. After first heat- ing to 600” C IRM increased between a hundred to a thousand times and the Curie temperature of newly created minerals could be determined (Vincenz and Jelehska, 1985; Jelenska, 1985). Maghemite shows a decrease in susceptibility after heatin

increased between a hundred to a thousand times and the Curie temperature of newly created minerals could be determined (Vincenz and Jelehska, 1985; Jelenska, 1985). Maghemite shows a decrease in susceptibility after heating above 300 o C due to conversion to hema- tite (Lowrie and Heller, 1982). Such a decrease (Fig. 2b, c) or hematite is not observed, excluding the presence of maghemite. The observed mag- netite might be of primary origin or derived from pyrite. The latter possibility has been considered because of the observation that during the heating of rock up to 600 o C new magnetite was created, very often together with pyrrhotite. Both might be a product of the conversion of pyrite which was present in the unheated rock. According to Ward (1970) and Schwarz (1975) slow oxidation of hexagonal pyrrhotites leads to the formation of monoclinic magnetic pyrrhotite and magnetite. Introduction In spite of numerous geological and paleomag- netic studies, the plate and microplate motions that have given rise to the Variscan belt are still ill understood. Tarling has recently exposed the problems and limits of Paleozoic paleomagnetism [1]. The mean Devonian and Carboniferous virtual paleopoles of northern Europe are very affected by Late Variscan overprints, and the commonly accepted paleopositions of Europe during Hercynian times are probably not definitive [2]. In the same way, the latest paleomagnetic models proposed for the Variscan belt cannot be consid- ered as satisfying because they are often based on ill-dated remagnetizations [3,4]. Concerning the African plate, the lack of data is dramatic. Recent paleomagnetic and radiometric studies on the so- called "Msissi norite" in southern Morocco reject the unique Late Devonian paleopole of Africa [5] and question the existence of a widespread Hercynian ocean. With exception of the SSW A and A' directions which indicate the paleosouth direction, there is an undetermination for the other directions. Several arguments are in favour of a reversed polarity of the WSW B direc- tions. First, a 50 ° clockwise rotation needs less energy than a 130 ° counterclockwise rotation, and this in a rather short period of about 10 Ma (310-300 Ma). In Roannais, a clockwise rotation of the series was observed during the interval defined by the emplacement of two B magnetiza- tions, the first carried by magnetite, the second by hematite. As geological considerations exclude a local rotation, it is tempting to attribute this devi- ation to a more general motion, corresponding partially to the 50 ° clockwise rotation. In other massifs of the Variscan belt arguments exist in favour of Late Hercynian clockwise rotations, e.g. in the Armorican Massif, the Ardenne, the Vosges and the Black Forest [2,8-10]. belt; these granites have been dated by the K-Ar method at 110-125 Ma [13]. The age of the Miyako Group is thus estimated to lie between 100 and 110 Ma. Tosha [1] recently sampled the Miyako Group at 9 sites, and obtained paleomagnetic results for six sites spread over less than 2 km. We have extended the sampling to an additional 10 sites, spread over approximately 25 km along the sea coast. Ninety cores were drilled from nine sites using a portable drill. Orientation was performed with a magnetic compass and, whenever possible, with a solar com- pass. 2. Paleomagnetic data In each site, two pilot specimens were subjected to thermal demagnetization in steps of 40 °C and two other pilot specimens to alternating field (AF) demagnetization in steps of 5 mT. All magnetic measurements were done with a two-component CTF cryogenic magnetometer and included a cor- 323 rection (when necessary) for (very weak) spurious magnetization of the sample holder. The noise level of the magnetometer is estimated to be about (or less than) 10-11A m 2 (corresponding to a magnetization of 10-6A m -1 for a sample of volume 10 cm3). This direction is found to coincide with that of most older plutonic and sedimentary rocks of Devonian to lower Cretaceous age. It is also identical with the westerly pre-folding direction which is preserved in many Oligocene (20-40 Ma) formations from Northeast Japan [1,2]. In contrast, all recent formations (0-17 Ma) have been magnetized in the direction of the present axial dipole field. Only the Oligocene and Miocene results appear to be primary, or at least pre-folding. The Miyako sulfide-bearing sediments and lower Cretaceous (110-125 Ma) magnetite-bearing granites could either still bear a primary magnetiza- tion or be completely remagnetized by a low temperature chemical event. Evidence for such events is now found in many places, and as close as South Korea. Available data constrain the Oligo-Miocene history of Northeast Japan and indicate at least 20/30 o counterclockwise rotation with respect to mainland Asia during the opening of the Sea of Japan. On the other hand, the pre-40 Ma history of Northeast Japan is not well constrained and three models are proposed which are compatible with various interpretations of the data. It is also identical with the westerly pre-folding direction which is preserved in many Oligocene (20-40 Ma) formations from Northeast Japan [1,2]. Rock types include prominent quartz-arenites, con- glomerates, diamictites and mudstones, as well as shales. Maximum unblocking temperatures no higher than 580 ° C, and generally linear decay to the origin after removal of an insignificant low-blocking temperature compo- nent, characterized the stable samples of these formations. Both northwesterly downward and southeasterly upward directions were observed (Figs. 8, 9) in a total of 9 samples from 3 sites. Introduction Because the paleomagnetic data base for the Paleozoic of Gondwana is relatively poor, many uncertainties exist about the plate motions and paleogeographic positions of this supercontinent. As a consequence, models for Paleozoic continent- continent collisions involving the present Circum- Atlantic continents are very poorly constrained. The reasons for the paucity of data are manifold, and include a scarcity in general of Paleozoic rocks in the cratonic parts of the Gondwana conti- nents, more particularly a lack of formations sui- table for paleomagnetic analysis, a lack of precise ages for the rocks that do exist, the possibility of widespread remagnetization, and uncertainties about the positions of non-cratonic areas, such as the eastern Australian fold belts, which have yielded several paleomagnetic results previously. * Now at: Department of Earth Sciences, University of Ox- ford, Parks Road, Oxford, OX1 3PR, United Kingdom. Tankard and Hobday [20] interpreted the de- positional environment of the Table Mountain, Bokkeveld and Witteberg Groups as typical for a basin that evolved as the failed arm of a major rift system, with more or less continuous Paleozoic subsidence leading to the immense thickness of at least 7000 m in a miogeosynclinal setting. Rock types include prominent quartz-arenites, con- glomerates, diamictites and mudstones, as well as shales. While they are locally hematite bearing, such generally coarse rock types do not usually provide good paleomagnetic data and the finer- grained strata have been preferred for sampling. Even so, we have encountered highly unstable magnetic behaviour in many of the formations sampled, and only four formations gave magneti- zations of presumably Paleozoic age (the Graaf- water, Pakhuis, Cedarberg Shale Formations and the Bokkeveld Group; see Fig. 2). Below, geologi- cal descriptions are given for these four forma- tions only. The Graafwater Formation is the third oldest in the Table Mountain Group. It was sampled along Chapman's Peak Drive, south of Cape Town (Fig. 3). The areal extent of the coherent tectonic unit of South- west Japan is now disputed [16], and consequently paleomagnetic data compiled from the entire area of Southwest Japan, as defined geographically, provide unwanted information about the different block motions from regions marginal to the coher- ent block. Our study area is limited to the central part of this area, so that our data are appropriate for obtaining the characteristic APWP for the Southwest Japan block. Extensive volcanic activity accompanied with intrusion of plutonic rocks occurred in the Inner Zone of Southwest Japan between the late Meso- zoic and Tertiary periods (Fig. 1). Because the rifting of the Japan arc is presumed to have occurred as recently as the middle Miocene [5,10,11], the geomorphological and geological evidence has not been obscured by subsequent geological activity. The Japan arc thus provides an opportunity to study the geodynamics of the rifting of the continental sliver. 0012-821X/87/$03.50 :,~' 1987 Elsevier .Science Publishers B.V. One of the most important features of the rifting process is the mode of opening of a basin in association with rifting of the sliver from its mother continent, because the rifting mode sheds light on the understanding for the origin of the forces affecting the continental margin and for the mechanical resistance of the continental litho- sphere. Some models have been proposed for the rifting of the continental sliver; (1) fan shape opening mode of the back arc basin [12], (2) parallel opening mode of the Atlantic type [13], and (3) pull-apart basin [14,15]. Drifting motion of a continental sliver is the clue to inference for the opening mode, because the difference between the fan shape mode and the other two modes can be distinguished by the degree of rotation during drift of the sliver. The areal extent of the coherent tectonic unit of South- west Japan is now disputed [16], and consequently paleomagnetic data compiled from the entire area of Southwest Japan, as defined geographically, provide unwanted information about the different block motions from regions marginal to the coher- ent block. Our study area is limited to the central part of this area, so that our data are appropriate for obtaining the characteristic APWP for the Southwest Japan block. Extensive volcanic activity accompanied with intrusion of plutonic rocks occurred in the Inner Zone of Southwest Japan between the late Meso- zoic and Tertiary periods (Fig. 1). The volcanic rocks are mostly welded pyroclastics with interbedded lavas and elastic rocks. The Yama- guchi to G8 river areas have been geologically mapped in detail, and extensive radiometric dat- ing has been done using the K-Ar, Rb-Sr and fission-track methods [17-20]. Here we report new results from upper Paleo- zoic formations from the eastern portions of the Atacama Desert of northern Chile to further con- strain the nature of displacements and rotations that may have occurred in the Mesozoic and Cenozoic within the Andes. These data come from the high western flank of the main cordillera, and help to resolve the extent of discordances along the western flanks of the central Andes that has thus far been principally documented for coastal regions. Soft-sediment deformation within the area is widespread, with occasional well-developed slump structures. Introduction The Siwalik Series of fluvial molasse deposits exposed in the Potwar area of northern Pakistan present an unparalleled opportunity for studies of foredeep sedimentation. These molasse deposits preserve a 17 million year record of the Himalayan orogeny. Foredeep sedimentation was sequentially disrupted during the Late Pliocene and Pleisto- cene [1]. Recent studies of the magnetic polarity stratigraphy of the Siwaliks, coupled with fission track dating of volcanic tuff horizons has enabled the construction of a broad chronological frame- work for Siwalik sedimentation and tectonic dis- ruption [2-4]. The long sequences of Siwalik sediments pre- sent an excellent opportunity for study of the palaeomagnetic record of terrestrial sediments. The deposition rates are generally high, of the order of 0.2-0.5 m/ka [5], and these rates allow detailed studies of magnetization to be undertaken, using close sampling intervals, equivalent to relatively short periods of geological time. The importance of the section lies not only in the inferences that can be drawn from the palaeomagnetic study of the sediments but also in the fact that a stone artefact and other pieces of struck stone were found in situ near the base of the section. Finds of stone artefacts in situ in the Siwaliks have been reported previously from the eastern Potwar [6], but, given the stratigraphic and tectonic setting, the Soan context is likely to be of greater antiquity. The section has significant archaeological importance, and the measurements of magnetic polarity stratigraphy have the poten- tial to provide a chronological framework for these artefacts. 2. Later workers established lithostrati- graphic units and these units form the current basis for Siwalik stratigraphy [8]. Raynolds [11] argues that the tectonic evolu- tion of the Soan area comprised two phases. First, during the interval 3.5-2.5 Ma, the Riwat Fault was active, uplifting the southern part of the area and accounting for a gap in the sedimentary se- quence on the southern limb of the fold during the lower Gauss Chron. This movement had ceased by ca. 2.4 Ma. Second, during the interval 2.1-1.9 Ma, the main folding event of the syncline oc- curred. Although deformation appears to have ceased by 1.6 Ma, some of the palaeomagnetic data presented by Burbank and Raynolds [1] sug- gest that the syncline has undergone a 10-20 ° counterclockwise rotation between about 1.8 Ma and the present.
